name: Anan
title: One of the heads of the people who sealed the covenant
summary: Anan is mentioned among the people's leaders who set their seal on the written covenant with God, as described in Nehemiah 10. When the Jewish community returned from the Babylonian exile, it underwent a deep spiritual renewal. After Ezra's public reading of the Torah and an extensive confession of sin, this renewal culminated in a solemn sealing of the covenant. By setting their seal on the covenant, Anan and the other leaders committed themselves to obeying the Mosaic Law, keeping the Sabbath holy, refraining from marriage with surrounding peoples, and supporting temple service through tithes and offerings. His participation testifies to the broad support among the people's leaders for a binding return to faithfulness toward God's commands.

keyEvents.title: Sealing of the Covenant
keyEvents.description: Anan was among the heads of the people who placed their seal on the written covenant with God, committing themselves to keep God's law and commandments.

keyEvents.title: The People's Renewed Commitment
keyEvents.description: Together with priests, Levites, and other leaders, Anan took part in the collective commitment to remain separate from the surrounding nations and live faithfully according to the Law of Moses.

keyEvents.title: Provisions of the Covenant
keyEvents.description: As part of the sealed covenant, Anan joined others in committing to sanctify the Sabbath, refrain from intermarriage with foreigners, and support temple service through tithes and offerings.

versions.summary: Anan was one of the leaders of the Jewish people who placed his seal on the covenant with God during the time of Nehemiah. He is mentioned among those who committed themselves to follow God's law after returning from the Babylonian exile. His role was to confirm the people's renewed commitment to the Lord.
versions.title: One Who Sealed the Covenant
versions.reason: [major] Anan is mentioned in Nehemiah 10:26 in some translations, but in the Hebrew text (and many translations) the name Anan appears in Neh 10:26. It should be verified that this is the correct verse. In the Hebrew text, Anan is listed in Neh 10:26 (or 10:27 depending on verse numbering). Some Bible editions have different verse numbering in Neh 10.; [minor] The event "The People's Renewed Commitment" is more a general description of the covenant renewal in which all participated, not a specific event tied to Anan personally. It is acceptable as context, but the description should clarify that this applied to the entire community.; [minor] The Sabbath commitment (v. 31) is a collective provision in the covenant. It is somewhat speculative to make this a separate key event specifically for Anan, since he is mentioned only as one of many who sealed the covenant.; [minor] Similarly, the commitment to temple service is collective. Listing verses 32 and 39 as separate verses in an array could be misinterpreted – this is a range (32–39), but as it stands now, it looks like only verses 32 and 39.; [minor] The role "leader" is somewhat vague. It is not certain that Anan was a leader in the traditional sense; he is listed among "the heads of the people" who sealed the covenant. A more precise role could be "head of the people" or "covenant sealer."; [minor] Footnotes are missing. It would be helpful to have a linguistic note about the name Anan (Hebrew: עָנָן, meaning "cloud"), as well as a historical context note about the covenant renewal under Nehemiah.; [minor] The summary is fine, but could include a brief explanation of the context – that this took place after Ezra's reading of the law and the people's repentance over their sins.

versions.summary: Anan was one of the heads of the people who placed his seal on the covenant with God during the time of Nehemiah. He is listed among those who committed themselves to follow God's law after returning from the Babylonian exile. The renewal of the covenant took place after Ezra's public reading of the Law and the people's confession of sin, and included a commitment to keep the Law of Moses, observe the Sabbath, avoid intermarriage with foreigners, and support temple service.
versions.title: One of the heads of the people who sealed the covenant
versions.reason: [major] Anan is mentioned in Nehemiah 10:26 in some verse numbering systems, but in the Hebrew text (and many translations) Nehemiah 10 is shifted so that the list of names begins at verse 1 (Hebrew 10:2). In many translations Anan appears in Neh 10:26, but this should be verified against the Hebrew numbering. Most translations place Anan in Neh 10:26, so this can be accepted, though it is worth noting that the Hebrew text has a different verse division (Neh 10:1 in Hebrew = Neh 9:38 in many translations).; [minor] Typo: 'deltok' should be 'deltok' (this is correct Bokmål). However, the phrasing is somewhat awkward - 'deltok Anan i' is grammatically correct.; [minor] The summary is good and informative, but it resembles the previous version (version 1) in structure and wording. It could usefully be made more distinct to avoid reusing previously rejected text.; [minor] The covenant stipulations extend over many verses (Neh 10:30-39). Referring only to verses 30, 31, 32, and 39 is selective but acceptable. Verses 33-38 also contain important provisions concerning temple service and tithing.

After returning from the Babylonian exile, the Jewish community underwent a spiritual renewal that culminated in a solemn sealing of the covenant. This took place following Ezra's public reading of the Torah and a thorough confession of sin by the people. Neh 10:27 is an alternative reference depending on verse numbering. footnotes.text: The name Anan (Hebrew: עָנָן, 'ānān) means "cloud" or "cloud cover" in Hebrew. It is related to the Hebrew word for cloud used several times in the Old Testament, including regarding the pillar of cloud that led the Israelites in the wilderness (Exod 13:21–22). As a personal name, it occurs only in Neh 10:26.

The covenant renewal in Nehemiah 10 took place after Ezra's public reading of the Law of Moses (Neh 8) and the people's collective confession of sin and prayer (Neh 9). Those who sealed the covenant represented three groups: priests, Levites, and heads of the people. Anan is listed among the heads of the people, suggesting that he held a certain social or political position in post-exilic Judah.

The sealing of the covenant involved a written, legally binding commitment. In the ancient Near East, the use of seals was a well-known legal means to confirm documents, agreements, and contracts. Archaeological finds of numerous seals and seal impressions (bullae) from Iron Age Judah confirm this practice and give the sealing in Nehemiah 10 a formal and solemn character.

The post-exilic covenant renewal in Nehemiah 10 can be seen as a continuation of a long biblical tradition of covenant renewals, from Joshua's covenant renewal at Shechem (Josh 24) to Josiah's reform covenant (2 Kgs 23). Theologically, it emphasizes the people's responsibility to actively renew their commitment to God in every generation.

In rabbinic tradition, the covenant renewal under Nehemiah was regarded as a decisive moment for the consolidation of Jewish identity after the exile. The commitment to avoid intermarriage and to keep the Sabbath holy became central markers of identity that characterized Jewish practice in the centuries that followed.
